q: What type does the compiler give to const d = "open"?
why: A const cannot change, so the compiler keeps the exact value: "open". A let can change, so c is the wider type string. I ran both with tsc 7.0.2.

q: The tuple type [string, number] means an array of any length that holds strings and numbers.
why: No. A tuple has a fixed length and a type for each place. Reading t[2] gives: Tuple type '[string, number]' of length '2' has no element at index '2'.

q: In strict mode, which of these usually need a type that you write yourself?
options: A function parameter with no default value, such as text in shout(text)
An empty array inside an object that you will push items into, such as { items: [] }
why: The compiler cannot work out a parameter that has no value to look at, so it reports an implicit any. It also types an empty array in an object as never[]. n and names have a first value to infer from.

q: Put these types in order, from the widest to the most exact.
why: string allows any text. "open" | "closed" allows two texts. "open" allows exactly one text. A narrower type catches more mistakes.

q: To keep { mode: "dark" } as the exact text "dark" and make it read-only, write the object and then: as ______ (one word)
why: as const stops the widening. The property becomes readonly mode: "dark", so a function that only accepts "dark" or "light" takes it without an error.

q: A function has the parameter text: any and calls text.toUpperCase(). What happens with shout(42)?
options: It compiles, then crashes when it runs: text.toUpperCase is not a function
The compiler reports an error on the call
why: any switches the checking off, so tsc says nothing about the number. Node then throws TypeError: text.toUpperCase is not a function. With text: string the call is a compile error.
